metadata.name: Ecodesign for Swift
metadata.description: Ecodesign rules for Swift code: battery-aware sensors, timers and background work, reused sessions that respect Low Data Mode, downsampled images, SwiftUI object lifetime, bounded Core Data fetches, no blocking of the main thread.

energie.name: Swift — device energy
energie.description: On a phone the energy is the user's battery, and the sensors are the expensive part (RGESN UX/Algorithms).

rules.title: Sensor left running
rules.description: Location, motion and Bluetooth scanning keep power-hungry hardware awake. Started and never stopped, they drain a battery in the background for a screen the user closed an hour ago.
rules.recommendation: Stop the updates as soon as the screen or the task that needed them goes away, ask for the coarsest accuracy that works, and prefer significant-change monitoring over continuous updates.
rules.note: One stop call anywhere in the file silences the rule. That is usually right, since start and stop are normally written as a pair, but a file starting several sensors needs each one stopped.

rules.title: Timer used to poll
rules.description: A repeating timer that re-fetches state runs whether or not anything changed, wakes the radio, and prevents the device from settling into a low-power state.
rules.recommendation: Drive the refresh from an event: a push notification, a WebSocket, a delegate callback. Where a timer is unavoidable, invalidate it when the view disappears and widen the interval.
rules.note: One invalidate() anywhere in the file silences the rule. Check that the timer flagged here is the one being invalidated, and that it happens when the view goes away.

rules.title: Highest location accuracy requested
rules.description: kCLLocationAccuracyBest and BestForNavigation keep GPS powered at full rate. Most features need a street or a city, which Wi-Fi and cell positioning give for a fraction of the energy.
rules.recommendation: Ask for the coarsest accuracy the feature needs (kCLLocationAccuracyHundredMeters, kCLLocationAccuracyKilometer, or reduced accuracy), and raise it only while the user is navigating.
rules.note: Turn-by-turn navigation and fitness tracking legitimately need the best accuracy. The question is whether this feature does.

rules.title: Location kept running in the background
rules.description: allowsBackgroundLocationUpdates lets location run after the app leaves the screen. Without pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically or a stop, GPS stays on for hours.
rules.recommendation: Prefer significant-change or visit monitoring in the background. If continuous updates are required, set pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically and an activityType so the system can pause them.
rules.note: The rule stays silent when the file lets the system pause updates or uses significant-change monitoring.

rules.title: Timer with no tolerance
rules.description: A timer without tolerance fires at the exact instant, so the system cannot group its wake-up with others. Apple's Energy Efficiency Guide asks for a tolerance of at least 10% of the interval.
rules.recommendation: Set timer.tolerance to at least a tenth of the interval, or pass tolerance: to Timer.publish.

example.good:
let t = Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval: 10, repeats: true) { _ in check() }
t.tolerance = 2

rules.note: One tolerance anywhere in the file silences the rule. A one-shot timer gains little from it.

rules.title: Screen kept awake
rules.description: isIdleTimerDisabled = true stops the screen from dimming and locking. The display is the largest energy draw on a phone, and it stays on for as long as the flag is set.
rules.recommendation: Set it only while the feature that needs it runs (video playback, navigation), and set it back to false when that ends or the view disappears.
rules.note: The rule stays silent when the same file sets the flag back to false.

rules.title: Heavy background task that does not wait for power
rules.description: A BGProcessingTaskRequest is meant for long work: indexing, cleanup, model updates. Without requiresExternalPower it can run on battery while the user sleeps.
rules.recommendation: Set requiresExternalPower = true (and requiresNetworkConnectivity only if needed) so the work runs while the device charges.

example.good:
let request = BGProcessingTaskRequest(identifier: id)
request.requiresExternalPower = true

rules.note: One requiresExternalPower = true anywhere in the file silences the rule. Work that must finish overnight on battery (a backup the user asked for) can keep it off on purpose.

ressources.name: Swift — resources and I/O
ressources.description: Reuse sessions, stream large data, keep the main thread free (RGESN Backend/Frontend).

rules.title: Main thread blocked
rules.description: A synchronous wait on the main thread freezes the interface: nothing renders, nothing responds, and the user taps again, which queues more work for the same result.
rules.recommendation: Keep the main thread for the interface. Move the work to a background queue or an async task, and update the UI when it returns.

example.good: Task { let d = await load(); await MainActor.run { render(d) } }

rules.title: Remote resource loaded synchronously and whole
rules.description: Data(contentsOf:) on a web URL downloads the whole response on the calling thread, with no cache, no timeout control and nothing on screen until the last byte lands. On the main thread it freezes the interface for as long as the network takes.
rules.recommendation: Fetch with a shared URLSession (data(from:) or a download task for large files), which reuses connections, honours the HTTP cache and runs off the main thread.
rules.note: Only a URL built from a string literal or an http(s) address is matched. Reading a local file whole is usually fine for small, bounded files (settings, a JSON store, a bundled resource), so the rule no longer flags Data(contentsOf: fileURL).

rules.title: URLSession built per request
rules.description: A session created for each call loses its connection pool and its cache: every request redoes DNS and the TLS handshake, on a radio that costs more energy the longer it stays awake.
rules.recommendation: Share one session for the app or the service, configured once with its cache policy and timeouts.
rules.note: A session held in a static let or a lazy var is exactly the recommendation, so the rule stays silent as soon as the file declares one.

rules.title: Network session ignores Low Data Mode
rules.description: Low Data Mode and expensive networks (cellular, personal hotspot) are the user telling apps to hold back. A session that never sets allowsConstrainedNetworkAccess or allowsExpensiveNetworkAccess downloads the same on a metered link as on Wi-Fi.
rules.recommendation: For prefetching, sync and large media, set allowsConstrainedNetworkAccess = false (and allowsExpensiveNetworkAccess = false where it fits), and fall back to a lighter request when it fails with constrained network.
rules.note: Requests the user explicitly asked for may go through anyway. The point is background and optional traffic.

rules.title: Image decoded at full size for a small display
rules.description: UIImage(data:) and NSImage(contentsOf:) decode every pixel. A 12-megapixel photo shown as a 100-point thumbnail takes about 48 MB once decoded, for a few kilobytes on screen.
rules.recommendation: Downsample to the display size with CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex (kCGImageSourceThumbnailMaxPixelSize) or preparingThumbnail(of:), and cache the result.
rules.note: A full-size view, an editor or an image already sized for its slot is fine. The rule stays silent when the file downsamples.

rules.title: Observed object created by the view
rules.description: @ObservedObject var model = Model() builds a new object every time SwiftUI recreates the view, which can be many times a second. Each new object redoes its setup: network calls, file reads, subscriptions.
rules.recommendation: Use @StateObject (or @State with an @Observable class) for an object the view owns, and @ObservedObject only for one passed in.

rules.title: Core Data fetch with no limit
rules.description: An NSFetchRequest with no fetchLimit or fetchBatchSize loads every matching object into memory, the Core Data equivalent of SELECT * without LIMIT.
rules.recommendation: Set fetchBatchSize for lists, fetchLimit when you need a few rows, propertiesToFetch for a subset of fields, or count(for:) when you only need the number.
rules.note: One limit anywhere in the file silences the rule, so a file with several fetches needs each checked.

rules.title: UserDefaults synchronize()
rules.description: synchronize() is deprecated and forces a write the system already schedules. Called after every change, it adds disk writes for nothing.
rules.recommendation: Remove the call. UserDefaults saves on its own.
